title: Gangtok on a budget: a good trip for less
meta_description: How to do Gangtok for ₹2,000–3,000 a day: shared jeeps and SNT buses, cheap stays, momo-and-thali meals, free sights and the add-ons worth skipping.
summary: A careful traveller can do Gangtok for about ₹2,000–3,000 a person a day, indicative 2026. The savings come from four habits: shared jeeps and SNT buses instead of reserved cars, a shared vehicle seat for Tsomgo, local food over hotel menus, and travelling outside the May–June and October peaks.

sections.heading: Where the money actually goes
paras: Most Gangtok budgets are not broken by hotels or food. They are broken by vehicles. A reserved car from Bagdogra, a half-day sightseeing package, a Tsomgo car and a drop back to the plains can add up to ₹15,000–20,000 for a family before anyone has eaten a momo. Two people sharing a room can halve that bill by riding with the locals on at least two of those four legs.
Here is what a frugal day and a comfortable day look like per person, sharing a room. These are indicative 2026 ranges, and prices rise in May, June and the October holidays.

sections.heading: Getting up the hill for under ₹600
paras: From Siliguri, shared jeeps leave from the Sikkim Nationalised Transport (SNT) terminus on Hill Cart Road and from the Panitanki More area through the morning. A seat costs ₹400–600 and the trip takes 4–5 hours on NH10 along the Teesta. SNT's own buses cost ₹275–500 and leave at set times; book a seat a day ahead in season. Both drop you at Deorali, about 2 km below MG Marg, where a local shared taxi to the centre costs ₹20–40.

Leave Siliguri before 1 pm. After that, shared jeeps thin out and you may be pushed into a reserved car at ₹4,000–5,500. If you land at Bagdogra, a shared auto or app cab to Siliguri town and a shared jeep onward still beats a reserved airport car for a couple. For families of four or more, a reserved car starts to make sense. Shared fares change with fuel prices, so check current status before you travel.

Plan the return the same way. Buy your seat back to Siliguri at the Deorali counter the afternoon before, and ask for a departure that gives you at least two hours' margin before a train from NJP or a flight from Bagdogra. In monsoon, make that margin a full spare day.

sections.heading: Sleeping cheap without sleeping badly
paras: Gangtok has hundreds of small hotels, and the cheapest are not always the best value. A room on Tibet Road, Paljor Stadium Road or around Development Area keeps you within a 10–15 minute walk of MG Marg, which saves ₹100–200 a day in taxis. Rooms right on the highway near Deorali look cheap but cost you a taxi every time you go out.

Budget hotels such as Hotel Sonam Delek on Tibet Road and Mintokling Guest House on Bhanu Path run at roughly ₹1,800–4,500 a room night, indicative 2026, depending on season and room. Ask three questions before you book: is there hot water all day, is there a heater in winter, and how many stairs to the room. Gangtok is built on a slope, and a cheap fifth-floor room with no lift is hard work with luggage.
Between mid-June and September, and again from January to early March, many hotels drop rates sharply. Ask for the walk-in rate, not the website rate.

sections.heading: Eating well for ₹400–600 a day
paras: Gangtok is one of the easiest hill towns in India to eat cheaply. A plate of momos costs ₹60–150, a bowl of thukpa or thenthuk ₹80–180, and a full rice-dal-sabzi thali ₹150–300, indicative 2026. Small eateries on the lanes below MG Marg and around Lal Bazaar serve the locals and charge local prices. The restaurants on MG Marg itself charge more for the view of the street.

Breakfast is the easy saving. Many cheaper hotels do not include it, and a hotel breakfast can cost ₹250–400. A tea shop with sel roti, aloo dum and tea will feed you for under ₹100. Carry a refillable bottle; most hotels will fill it with filtered water, and that saves ₹60–100 a day on bottled water in a state that discourages plastic.

sections.heading: Free and nearly free things to do
paras: Some of the best hours in Gangtok cost nothing. These are the ones we send budget travellers to first. Entry fees, where they exist, are small and change from time to time, so treat them as indicative.

Monasteries in and around Gangtok do not charge to enter the courtyards, but a small offering of ₹10–20 at the altar is customary and welcome. Walk clockwise around stupas and prayer wheels, take off your shoes where you see others do so, and ask before photographing inside a prayer hall. Most morning prayers start early, so arrive between 6 and 8 am if you want to hear the chanting.
list: MG Marg in the evening: a car-free street of about 1 km with benches down the middle. Free.
Enchey Monastery, about 3 km above MG Marg on the Nathu La road: a Nyingma monastery whose present building dates from 1909. Free; dress modestly.
Do Drul Chorten, the large white stupa built in 1945, ringed by 108 prayer wheels. Free.
Namgyal Institute of Tibetology next to the Chorten: one of the best small museums in the Himalaya. Entry around ₹10–50.
Ridge Park and the walk past the palace gate at the top of town. Free, best in March and April when the trees flower.
Lal Bazaar on a Sunday morning, when village sellers bring greens, chhurpi and dried fish to the haat. Free to wander.
Hanuman Tok and Ganesh Tok for mountain views on a clear morning; walkable if your knees are good, or a cheap shared taxi.

sections.heading: Sightseeing: shared seats and smart cuts
paras: The classic Gangtok half-day car tour costs ₹1,800–3,500 per vehicle, indicative 2026. Split between four people it is fair value. For a couple it is not, because most of the stops on the list are within walking distance of the centre or a ₹20–40 shared taxi away. Do the town on foot and save the car budget for Tsomgo.

For Tsomgo Lake and Baba Mandir, a shared seat in a tour vehicle costs ₹800–1,300, against ₹4,500–6,500 for a whole car. Your hotel or a travel desk on MG Marg can put you in a vehicle with other travellers. Rumtek is another easy saving: a shared taxi seat costs ₹60–120 against ₹1,200–2,000 for a reserved return trip.

Skip the add-ons that drain money at the lake. Yak rides cost ₹300–600, and coat and boot hire ₹100–300. In April or October a warm jacket from home is enough. Hire only if there is snow on the ground.

sections.heading: When to go for the lowest prices
paras: Rates in Gangtok follow school holidays across eastern India. Late May, June and the Durga Puja to Diwali weeks in October and November are the dearest. December can be busy around Christmas and New Year.

The cheapest months are mid-June to September and January to early March. Monsoon brings rain and NH10 landslides, so keep a spare day; winter brings cold nights and the chance of Nathu La closing after snow. Our pick for budget travellers is the first half of March or the second half of November: fair weather, clear views on many mornings, and hotels still willing to bargain. Check current status before you travel, since road and pass closures change week to week.

A simple three-night plan we give students and young couples: day one, shared jeep up from Siliguri and an evening on MG Marg; day two, a walking loop of the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology, Do Drul Chorten, Enchey Monastery and Ridge Park; day three, a shared seat to Tsomgo and Baba Mandir; day four, the morning shared jeep back down. Done this way, transport for the whole trip comes to about ₹1,800–2,800 per person, indicative 2026.

faqs.q: How much does a 3-day Gangtok trip cost on a budget
faqs.a: About ₹7,000–10,000 per person for three nights, twin sharing, indicative 2026, if you use shared jeeps from Siliguri, stay in a budget hotel near MG Marg, eat local and take a shared seat to Tsomgo. Add ₹2,000–4,000 if you want a reserved car for one day. Our Gangtok budget package starts around ₹9,500 per person with transfers arranged.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way from Siliguri to Gangtok
faqs.a: An SNT bus at ₹275–500, or a shared jeep seat at ₹400–600, indicative 2026. Both run from the SNT terminus on Hill Cart Road in Siliguri, and shared jeeps also leave from the Panitanki More area. Go before 1 pm, when departures thin out. Both drop you at Deorali, 2 km below MG Marg. Fares change with fuel prices, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is a shared Tsomgo tour worth it
faqs.a: Yes, for solo travellers and couples. A shared seat costs ₹800–1,300 against ₹4,500–6,500 for a whole car, indicative 2026, and you see the same lake and Baba Mandir. The trade-off is less control over stops and timing. Families of four or five usually pay about the same per head by booking their own car, and get more freedom for photos.

faqs.q: Which month is cheapest for Gangtok
faqs.a: July and August are cheapest, with many hotels discounting heavily, but rain and NH10 landslides make travel slow. For low prices with fair weather, we suggest early March or the second half of November. January and February are also cheap, though nights are cold and Nathu La may close after snow. Check current status before you travel in any of these months.

faqs.q: Can I see Gangtok without hiring a car
faqs.a: Yes. MG Marg, Lal Bazaar, the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology, Do Drul Chorten and Ridge Park are all walkable from the centre. Enchey Monastery and Hanuman Tok are a short shared-taxi ride or an uphill walk. Rumtek and Ranka have shared taxis at ₹60–120 a seat. You only really need a car for Tsomgo and Nathu La.

faqs.q: What do momos cost in Gangtok
faqs.a: Expect ₹60–150 a plate of six to ten, indicative 2026, depending on filling and place. Vegetable and cheese momos are cheapest; pork and beef cost more. Small places on the lanes below MG Marg and around Lal Bazaar charge less than the restaurants on MG Marg itself. A bowl of thukpa or thenthuk costs about ₹80–180.

faqs.q: Are budget hotels in Gangtok safe and clean
faqs.a: Most registered budget hotels near MG Marg are safe and reasonably clean, and Gangtok has a strong civic culture. Check recent reviews for hot water, damp walls and stairs, since many buildings have no lift. Ask for a room facing away from the road if you sleep lightly. Hotels collect the ₹50 Sikkim tourist fee at check-in; keep the receipt.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay for Tsomgo yak rides and coat hire
faqs.a: No. Both are optional. Yak rides cost ₹300–600 and coat and boot hire ₹100–300, indicative 2026. If you visit between April and November with a warm jacket, gloves and good shoes from home, you will not need to hire anything. Hire boots only if there is fresh snow, usually between December and March.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to book Gangtok sightseeing from Siliguri
faqs.a: Usually not. Only Gangtok-registered tourist vehicles are allowed on the Tsomgo and Nathu La permit routes, so a Siliguri car cannot do those trips. Book local sightseeing and Tsomgo in Gangtok through your hotel or a registered agent, and use the Siliguri car, if any, only for the transfer up and down.
